messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame Mensah, a 72-year-old African American Coast Guard serviceman who had spent decades around harbors, maintenance yards, and cutters, traced the beginning of his current difficulties to a toxic chemical exposure that occurred during a routine workday. He had been in an enclosed service area near stored industrial cleaning agents and fuel-related materials when a breach released a powerful chemical smell into the air. What stayed with him most was not only the burning in his throat and eyes, but the eerie stillness that came just beforehand. He remembered how the usual industrial hum seemed to drop away for a moment, how the room felt unnaturally quiet, and how in that silence he had the immediate sense that something was wrong. Then came the exposure itself: the sharp odor, the choking sensation, the panic in his body as he struggled to orient himself and get out. Even now, when he spoke about it, the scene did not come back as a general memory but as stark visual fragments, “like snapshots,” fixed images of the enclosed space, the containers, the air that suddenly seemed unbreathable.

In the weeks afterward, Kwame found that the event did not settle into the past. Instead, it returned in a repetitive, almost mechanical way, as though a film were running in his mind without his permission. He would be going about his day and suddenly see the scene again with photographic clarity. When this happened, he did not experience it as distant recollection. He felt flooded by it, so emotionally overcome that he had to stop whatever he was doing. At times he would fall silent mid-conversation or leave a task unfinished because he could feel himself losing control in the force of the memory. He had come to believe that if he let himself think about the exposure for more than a moment, he would not be able to handle what followed. Because of that, he worked hard to cut off thoughts before they developed, telling himself not to go there, not to picture the room, not to remember the smell.

What frightened Kwame almost as much as the memory itself was how alert he felt afterward, as if danger could announce itself anywhere. He found himself reacting to unusual silence with immediate alarm. In the Coast Guard setting, he was accustomed to meaningful sound—engines, radios, tools, movement, the ordinary noise of a working environment. When a corridor, dock space, or work room became too still, his body tensed before he had time to think. He would scan the area, waiting for something hazardous to happen. Even at home, where his wife expected him to rest, he could not fully let down his guard. A quiet house did not feel peaceful to him. It felt like the moment before disaster, and he remained watchful in his own living room, listening for signs that something was wrong.

Reminders brought strong physical reactions. A chemical odor, industrial cleaning supplies, or certain maintenance areas at work could set off a pounding heart and a surge of bodily distress so intense that he had to step away. He did not describe these moments as simple discomfort. To him, his body was telling him that the threat was back. Over time, this changed the way he moved through both work and home. He became more hesitant in enclosed work spaces and more uneasy during quiet stretches of a shift. His wife noticed that he was less able to tolerate even minor frustrations. He had come to believe that he could no longer manage the slightest upset, and this left him feeling diminished and older than he wanted to admit. Small disruptions that he once would have handled briskly now felt like proof that he was no longer steady.

As months passed, his view of the world grew increasingly stark. He was certain that danger was not exceptional but everywhere, waiting in places others treated as routine. Ordinary environments—his station, a storage area, even his own home—no longer felt reliably safe. This was part of what kept him on edge, but it also shaped his choices. He narrowed what he exposed himself to mentally and physically, trying to keep distance from anything that might bring the images back. The cost of that avoidance showed up in daily life. At work, he was less able to move through tasks with the old confidence his role had demanded. At home, his wife lived with a man who was present but vigilant, one ear always tuned to the possibility of trouble.

By the time he sought help, Kwame was exhausted by the repetition of it all: the film-like replay, the frozen images, the silence that made his whole body brace, the conviction that one upsetting moment could undo him. What finally brought him in was the sense that he could not continue living as though every quiet room concealed another exposure. He wanted relief from the constant readiness and from the memories that overwhelmed him so quickly, but he was also deeply afraid that speaking about the event directly would prove him right—that once he allowed himself to face it fully, he would not be able to cope.
